pages.text: DIETARY GUIDELINES CHAPTER 14 1 | Define and describe the Dietary Guidelines for Americans. 2 | Explain the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) nutrition programs that rely on the Dietary Guidelines. 3 | Define the key elements of healthy eating. 4 | Determine the dietary suggestions to align with healthy eating patterns. LEARNING OBJECTIVES ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 295

CHAPTER 14 | Dietary Guidelines ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 296 The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and US Department of Agriculture (USDA) create and update the Dietary Guidelines for Americans to promote sustainable, healthy food choices for lifelong health and good nutrition. With the aim of preventing chronic diseases such as cancer, hypertension, stroke, heart disease, and other chronic conditions, the guidelines address what to eat and what to avoid eating for optimal health. Foods available to American consumers today include fresh, packaged, and processed products. To make the best choices, it is important for consumers to read and understand food labels. Even the simplest food packaging includes a nutrition label, list of ingredients, and often nutrition and health benefit claims. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulates each of these elements for accuracy and effectiveness. The current dietary guidelines are useful for making healthy food choices and crafting a well- rounded diet. Nutrition coaches and fitness professionals can use these guidelines as the basis for helping clients develop healthier dietary habits to support their goals. Figure 14.1 Dietary Guidelines for Americans The first half of the 164-page Dietary Guidelines contains chapters related to various nutrition topics. The second half of the Dietary Guidelines contains the Dietary Guidelines Appendix with helpful tables of foods, nutrient sources, calorie intake, and more. In addition to nutrition, the Dietary Guidelines also contain information about physical activity recommendations. PURPOSE OF DIETARY GUIDELINES Dietary Guidelines are meant to guide the development of federal food, nutrition, and health policies and programs. The primary audiences are policy makers and nutrition health professionals, rather than the public. This publication is a critical tool used by professionals to help Americans make healthy choices in their daily lives with the goal of preventing chronic disease. The publication serves as the evidence-based foundation for nutrition education materials that the federal government creates for the public. For example, federal dietary guidance publications are required by law to be consistent with the Dietary Guidelines. US DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES (HHS): A US federal department that oversees public health, welfare, and civil rights issues. US DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE (USDA): A US federal department that manages programs for food, nutrition, agriculture, natural resources, and rural development. DIETARY GUIDELINES: Guidelines for healthy, lifelong eating habits for Americans two years of age and older. FOOD AND DRUG ADMINISTRATION (FDA): A US federal department that regulates the production and distribution of food, pharmaceuticals, tobacco, and other consumer products.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 297 The Dietary Guidelines are also used to guide USDA and HHS food programs as well as many other programs administered by federal departments, such as: • The USDA’s National School Lunch Program and School Breakfast Program • The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) • The Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) • The HHS Administration on Aging’s Older Americans Act Nutrition Services programs • Department of Defense and Department of Veterans Affairs food programs The Dietary Guidelines are also used to develop programs, policies, and communication by schools, community groups, and state/local governments. These organizations share the common goal of serving the public. The 2020-2025 Dietary Guidelines translate nutrition science into food-based guidance for a healthy and enjoyable diet. The focus is on disease prevention and long-term wellness. All Americans, regardless of individual health status, can benefit from making better food choices and developing healthy eating patterns. Thus, the Dietary Guidelines may be used or adopted by medical and nutrition professionals to encourage healthier habits in their clients. While these recommendations provide a strong, science-based framework for improving public health, complementary perspectives can help professionals apply the guidelines in ways that honor individual needs, preferences, and lived experiences. One such perspective is the Health at Every Size approach.

CHAPTER 14 | Dietary Guidelines ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 298 HEALTH AT EVERY SIZE – A WEIGHT-INCLUSIVE APPROACH While the Dietary Guidelines emphasize evidence-based recommendations for supporting health and preventing chronic disease, it is important to recognize that healthy eating patterns can look different for each individual. The Health at Every Size (HAES) framework offers a weight-inclusive perspective that shifts the focus from body weight as the primary indicator of health to overall well-being and sustainable health-promoting behaviors. The HAES approach is built on five core principles: 1 Weight inclusivity: Accepting and respecting the natural diversity of body shapes and sizes. 2 Health enhancement: Supporting access to information and services that improve overall well-being. 3 Respectful care: Addressing weight bias, stigma, and discrimination in healthcare and wellness settings. 4 Eating for well-being: Encouraging flexible eating patterns that are guided by hunger, satiety, nutritional needs, and pleasure. 5 Life-enhancing movement: Promoting enjoyable, accessible physical activity for people of all abilities and sizes. In practice, HAES encourages individuals to choose a variety of nutrient-rich foods they enjoy, move their bodies in ways that feel good rather than as punishment or solely for weight loss, and develop a positive relationship with food and eating that emphasizes nourishment, satisfaction, and cultural traditions. This approach also acknowledges the powerful role that culture, access, economics, and personal preference play in shaping dietary choices. For example, a client’s ability to follow certain recommendations from the Dietary Guidelines may be influenced by factors such as food costs, local availability of fresh produce, or time constraints. Recognizing these realities helps nutrition and health professionals create strategies that are not only nutritionally sound but also realistic and respectful of individual circumstances. When paired with the Dietary Guidelines, HAES offers a broader framework for promoting health. Nutrition coaches can use both to guide clients toward balanced eating patterns and healthful behaviors without making body weight the sole measure of progress or success. Together, these approaches support the overarching goal of the Guidelines: helping individuals achieve lifelong health and well-being through sustainable, positive lifestyle choices. HEALTH AT EVERY SIZE (HAES): A weight-inclusive approach that promotes health through enjoyable movement, flexible eating patterns, and respectful care, regardless of body size. Key principles include weight inclusivity, health enhancement beyond weight loss, eating for well-being, life-enhancing movement, and recognition of cultural and economic influences on food choices.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 299 FIVE FOCUS AREAS OF THE DIETARY GUIDELINES The Dietary Guidelines are organized progressively, starting with five core concepts which are followed up with more detailed guidelines for food choices. 1. Follow a healthy eating pattern across the life span. All food and beverage choices contribute to health. Choose an eating pattern at an appropriate calorie level to support nutrient needs and overall well-being. 2. Focus on variety, nutrient density, and food amounts. Choose a variety of nutrient-dense foods across and within all food groups in recommended amounts. 3. Limit added sugars, saturated fats and sodium. A balanced eating pattern includes fewer foods high in added sugars, saturated fats, and sodium. DID YOU KNOW? Sodium is a major target for physicians and the FDA to prevent and reduce chronic disease and hypertension. More than half of the sodium the average American consumes comes from: • Bread • Pizza • Canned soups • Burritos and tacos • Snack foods, like chips, crackers, and popcorn • Cheese • Cold cuts and deli meats 4. Shift to nutrient-rich food and beverage choices. Choose nutrient-dense options that reflect cultural traditions and personal preferences to make changes sustainable. 5. Support healthy eating patterns for all. Promote environments in the home, school, workplace, and community that make healthy choices accessible to everyone EATING PATTERN: The types of food and beverages an individual consumes. NUTRIENT DENSITY: The amount of nutrients in a food relative to the number of calories it provides, usually measured per 100 kilocalories.

CHAPTER 14 | Dietary Guidelines ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 300 DID YOU KNOW? A wide range of social and economic factors can influence a person’s eating patterns. These include economic status, cultural traditions, personal beliefs, food access, and many other external circumstances. Understanding these influences can help health professionals and educators create nutrition plans that are realistic, culturally respectful, and supportive of individual preferences. The Dietary Guidelines’ key recommendations work best when considered as a whole. Because foods and nutrients interact in complex ways, following only part of the recommendations may not capture the full benefits of a balanced eating pattern. LIMITING ADDED SUGARS A healthy eating pattern also involves being mindful of certain nutrients to limit, such as added sugars, certain fats, and sodium. These are areas of concern for public health in the United States, and setting reasonable limits can help support balanced eating within overall calorie needs. The recommendation for added sugars, those sugars not found naturally in whole foods, is to limit consumption to less than 10 percent of daily calories. This recommendation focuses on balance, allowing room for nutrient-dense foods first. LIMITING UNHEALTHY FATS Aim to keep saturated and trans fats limited to less than 10% of daily calories. When possible, choose unsaturated fats from foods such as nuts, seeds, fish, and plant oils. Research shows replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats is associated with reduced risk of cardiovascular disease. LIMITING SODIUM Sodium intake is recommended in quantities less than 2,300 milligrams per day. This is the Tolerable Upper Intake Level set by the National Academy of Medicine for people ages 14 and older. Refer to the Dietary Guidelines for Americans to view the recommendation for younger children. ADDED SUGARS: Any type of sugar that is added to a food or beverage when it is processed. This is compared to natural sugars found in whole foods, like fruit or milk.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 301 LIMITING ALCOHOL The current recommendation for alcohol consumption is to limit beverages to one drink per day for women and two per day for men, which is considered moderate drinking. Consuming more than the recommendation is considered heavy drinking and carries health risks. See the Dietary Guidelines for Americans for more information about who should abstain completely. THE FOOD PYRAMID TO MYPLATE A previous representation for the Dietary Guidelines, and one that most consumers still recognize, is the Food Pyramid. It acted as a visual tool to help individuals make better choices about food and creating a healthy eating pattern. Figure 14.2 The Food Pyramid The Food Pyramid used the number of servings per day of each food type to represent how much the average American should consume. It included servings for grains, vegetables, fruits, meats and other protein sources, dairy, and fats. The gradual thinning of the categories up the pyramid was intended to show that grains should be the focus of the diet, with each subsequent food group making up a smaller and smaller portion. Left out however, was a distinction between healthier whole grains and the processed, sugary foods like white pasta and cereals that are now known to have contributed to the US obesity epidemic. DID YOU KNOW? The USDA’s first dietary guidelines were published in 1980 and have been updated every five years since 1985.

CHAPTER 14 | Dietary Guidelines ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 302 Newer resources take fats, oils, and sweets completely out of the picture. Processed foods, desserts, and sugary beverages are energy-dense and lower in nutrient value, so individuals may choose to enjoy them less often while emphasizing nutrient-rich foods most of the time The food pyramid is also now thought to have put too little focus on fruits and vegetables and protein sources. The research that led to the transition from the Food Pyramid to MyPlate puts a greater focus on the Dietary Guidelines and choosing larger quantities of healthy whole foods. While the Food Pyramid was a popular resource, it is now considered dated. It has been replaced with the simplified, updated MyPlate representation. The official reason for the change is to simplify the visual tool and to promote healthy eating for a new generation of Americans. The guidelines presented are the same as those from the Dietary Guidelines, but the MyPlate tools and graphics are intended for use by the general population. They provide resources that nutrition, health, and fitness professionals can use to communicate effectively with clients. Figure 14.3 MyPlate Fruits Grains Dairy Protein Vegetables The new MyPlate is shaped like a plate with colorful fractions dedicated to dairy, vegetables, fruits, protein, and grains. This helps people visualize filling their plates at each meal with appropriate amounts of each food type. It is easy enough for a child to understand. Fats and sugars previously at the top of the Food Pyramid are left off the MyPlate graphic because of how they contribute to obesity in the overall population. Nutrition coaches and fitness professionals can use the MyPlate graphic as a teaching tool to explain healthy food choices and proportions to their clients. MYPLATE: The current visual nutrition guide published by the USDA Center for Nutrition Policy and Promotion.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 303 THE HARVARD HEALTHY EATING PLATE While MyPlate is the USDA’s primary visual guide for healthy eating, other evidence-based models provide additional insight. The Harvard Healthy Eating Plate, created by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, builds on similar principles while placing greater emphasis on the quality of foods chosen. This model encourages: • Filling half the plate with vegetables and fruits, with more vegetables than fruit and as much variety as possible. • Choosing whole grains such as brown rice, oats, and whole grain bread for about one quarter of the plate, while limiting refined grains like white bread and pasta. • Making healthy proteins such as fish, poultry, beans, and nuts about one quarter of the plate, and limiting red and processed meats. • Using healthy plant oils such as olive or canola for cooking and salads, while avoiding trans fats. • Drinking water, tea, or coffee in place of sugary beverages, and limiting milk and dairy to one to two servings per day. • Staying physically active as part of an overall healthy lifestyle. By pairing MyPlate’s clear portion visuals with Harvard’s emphasis on nutrient quality, nutrition coaches can give clients a more complete picture of healthy eating. Both tools can be adapted to fit individual preferences, cultural foodways, and varying levels of food access. FRUITS AND VEGGIES Half of a healthy plate should be fruits and vegetables. The focus should be on choosing whole fruits and vegetables which may include fresh, frozen, dried, or canned products with no additives. One can enjoy fruits as a sweet snack or dessert or with meals to increase daily intake. Vegetables should be varied in type and color. There are several healthful ways to prepare vegetables: sautéed, roasted, raw, or steamed. GRAINS Whole grains should fill up a quarter of a well-rounded plate. At least half the grains consumed daily should be whole grains. Any processed product is considered whole grain if the first or second item on the ingredients list is whole grains. Whole grain foods include brown rice, oatmeal, popcorn, whole wheat pasta, and whole grain breads.

CHAPTER 14 | Dietary Guidelines ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 304 PROTEINS Seafood, beans, unsalted nuts and seeds, eggs, poultry, and lean meats are all nutritious sources of protein. Including a variety of these foods supports muscle development, bone, blood, and skin health, and hormone production. Different protein sources provide different amino acids, so eating a mix helps the body get all it needs. DAIRY Opt for low-fat or fat-free products to help manage saturated fat intake while meeting calcium and vitamin D needs. Foods like sour cream, heavy cream, and regular cheese can be replaced with lower-fat varieties. Simple changes, such as using vegetable oils instead of butter or choosing water over sugary drinks, can add up to significant benefits over time. Nutrition coaches can support clients by encouraging small, manageable steps. Focusing on one change at a time, such as adding a fruit to each meal for a week or increasing vegetable portions, helps build confidence and consistency. Habits can take several weeks or even months to form, depending on the person and the behavior. Consistency is important, and focusing on gradual changes helps them become part of daily life. The Dietary Guidelines provide a valuable framework for guiding these gradual, lasting improvements.
